item.title: SlotFill: Repairing Lossy SoC Communication Traces for Post-Silicon Validation
item.description: arXiv:2611.31313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-silicon validation relies on traces of messages exchanged by SoC components, but trace buffers and monitors drop messages, often leaving no mark of what was lost. We present SlotFill, which puts each deleted message back in the right gap, with the right type and order. SlotFill gives every gap between the remaining messages a fixed number of slots, and a Transformer-based model fills each slot with a message or leaves it empty when nothing was deleted there, so the input never reveals how much was lost. The model also uses monitor fields (timestamps, transaction IDs, addresses) from surviving messages. On whole-program gem5 traces of 4- and 8-core systems (2.07 billion messages), SlotFill restores up to 97% of deleted messages exactly at 15% loss and up to 87% at 50% loss, and 76-83% at 15% loss when timestamps are coarse.
item.dc:creator: Tasnim Tabassum, Hao Zheng

item.title: ExitLUT: Boolean Early Exits for Efficient FPGA-Based Neural Network Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.31540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. In our CNN evaluation, fpgaConvNet is the static spatial-dataflow baseline, while ATHEENA is its softmax-based early exit extension. ExitLUT reduces ATHEENA's exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58$\times$ over the softmax path and eliminates decision-path DSP usage, while preserving accuracy and exit behavior. Rerunning design-space exploration reinvests these savings into the datapath, improving throughput by up to 4.08$\times$ over fpgaConvNet and 1.82$\times$ over ATHEENA. For LUT-based NNs, embedded ExitLUT exits achieve 1.41-1.89$\times$ average time-to-decision speedup over static NeuraLUT-Assemble designs with under 1% LUT overhead.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Cassidy, Marta Andronic, George A. Constantinides

item.title: Translation Validation of SystemVerilog-to-SystemC RTL Conversion by Reading the Generated C++
item.description: arXiv:2611.31674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: SystemC models of register-transfer level (RTL) designs are used for virtual platforms, firmware bring-up and simulation without a commercial license, and more of them now come from translators and language models. A wrong model usually compiles, and it usually agrees with the RTL. SystemVerilog evaluates an 8-bit sum in 8 bits while C++ evaluates it in 64, so a translation that forgets one truncation keeps a carry the RTL drops, and only inputs near the top of the range show it. I built svcc, an open-source SystemVerilog-to-SystemC converter, and my first check of its output read the generated C++ with SystemVerilog's rules. That check passed two wrong models. The check that replaced it gives the generated header the meaning C++17 and SystemC give it and turns undefined behavior into proof obligations. It prints what it read as SystemVerilog with every width change explicit, then proves that equivalent to a netlist of the source by induction over registers matched by name. On 50 author-written designs it proves 45 and reports 5 as outside its model. In a mutation experiment it accepted none of the 17 mutants that compiled SystemC showed to be wrong. Of 2,184 modules from 16 open-source code bases, 1,185 conversions match Verilator in random co-simulation and the check proves 600 of them. The same runs found defects in the front end, in svcc and in Verilator.
item.dc:creator: Mayur Kubavat

item.title: RTLDetective: Agentic RTL Debugging through Dataflow Analysis and Simulation-Guided Fault Localization
item.description: arXiv:2611.31709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promise in RTL debugging, yet accurately localizing functional errors and generating reliable repairs remain challenging. We propose RTLDetective, a multi-agent framework that integrates signal dependency analysis, simulation-guided fault localization, and knowledge-based reasoning for automated RTL debugging and repair. RTLDetective constructs signal dependency graphs from RTL code and extracts failure information from waveform traces. A lightweight localizer agent predicts expected intermediate signal values and evaluates them through targeted simulation interventions, iteratively probing signal dependencies to isolate suspicious logic and identify potential fault locations. A debug agent combines this evidence with static analysis, a curated knowledge base of hardware design principles and RTL bug patterns, and reasoning to generate corrected RTL. To reduce inference overhead, the framework reuses cached context across debugging iterations. We evaluate RTLDetective on the MEIC benchmark, achieving an 86.1% fix rate, 13.9 percentage points above the best baseline, while making fewer LLM calls.
item.dc:creator: Neusha Javidnia, Ruisi Zhang, Farinaz Koushanfar

item.title: MOSAIC: Memory-Organized Search with Anti-Imitation Crossover for Training-Free Microarchitecture Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.31733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also shows held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.
item.dc:creator: Kaushal Mhapsekar, Bita Aslrousta, Paula Contreras, Azam Ghanbari, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz

item.title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
item.description: arXiv:2611.31767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.
item.dc:creator: Kaushal Mhapsekar, Darsh Asher, Bita Aslrousta, Amna Hassan, Debayan Sengupta, Azam Ghanbari, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz

item.title: AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction
item.description: arXiv:2611.31876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Pengju Liu (Katie), Nuo Xu (Katie), Winso Chen (Katie), Peijun Li (Katie), Yang (Katie), Zhao, Yu Cao, Caiwen Ding

item.title: Native Block-Quantized Matrix Multiplication and Explicit K/V Residency with Dual-View Access for LLM Inference on RISC-V Vector Processors
item.description: arXiv:2611.31937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Some key execution states in large language model inference persist across multiple instructions and are difficult to express and exploit within RVV semantics centered on individual operations. We define specialization boundaries according to data-state lifetimes and propose Quantized Block Streams (QBS) and Attention/KV Context (AKV) while preserving RVV programmability. QBS organizes native-block format processing, block traversal, integer computation, and ordered FP32 accumulation into a unified execution process, whereas AKV maintains local K/V residency and supplies operand views aligned with the computation direction while leaving Attention arithmetic on RVV. Cycle-accurate RTL evaluation shows that QBS achieves geometric-mean speedups of 35.68x and 51.34x for projection Compute and Matmul, respectively, while AKV achieves a 1.45x geometric-mean speedup over Tiled RVV for Decode Attention. Compared with the baseline, the complete design increases total area by 12.65%; on the evaluated projection workloads, throughput per area and energy efficiency improve by 46.63x and 19.78x, respectively. Further evaluation demonstrates applicability across multiple block-quantization formats and across models with different Attention organizations.
item.dc:creator: Weiying Wang, Yuanyang Xiang, Zhiwei Zhang

item.title: Network-Guided Automated Synthesis of MAC Units for Neural Network Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.31986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In neural inference accelerators, multiply-accumulate (MAC) datapaths account for the majority of circuit area and critical-path delay, where operator-level numerical formats simultaneously dictate hardware overhead and quantization error. Yet no straightforward mapping exists between hardware cost and end-to-end network accuracy: logic synthesis transforms datapaths in a highly nonlinear manner, while numerical errors propagate and couple across layers. To address this disconnect, we present NAMSI, an automated network-aware MAC synthesis framework tailored for neural inference. NAMSI characterizes heterogeneous data formats using a format-distribution representation (FD) and leverages topology-aware accuracy and hardware-cost modeling (TaH), calibrated with actual post-synthesis Area-Delay Product (ADP) measurements, to jointly estimate coupled full-network accuracy and circuit cost. Furthermore, reversible lattice search (RLS) is introduced to tractably navigate the exponentially scaling design space. Evaluations across five neural networks on ImageNet-1K demonstrate that under post-training quantization (PTQ), NAMSI achieves 54.2%-60.4% reductions in post-synthesis MAC ADP compared with FP32 while retaining at least 99% of full-precision Top-1 accuracy, surpassing baseline approaches in both hardware efficiency and accuracy preservation.
item.dc:creator: Zhouyang Wu, Hongyang Pan, Chuyu Wang, Ji Zhuang, Keren Zhu, Xin Zhao, Xuan Zeng

item.title: Machine-Learning-Assisted Hybrid Cooling of a Raspberry Pi 5
item.description: arXiv:2611.32047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermal management is a critical challenge in compact computing platforms operating under sustained high computational loads. Elevated processor temperatures can lead to thermal throttling, degraded performance, and reduced reliability. This study develops and experimentally evaluates a smart hybrid heat sink that integrates passive thermal energy storage with active cooling for sustained device operation. The proposed design comprises an aluminum cavity containing paraffin wax as a phase change material (PCM) embedded within a copper foam and integrated with an adaptively controlled fan. Fan operation is guided by a Random Forest regression model trained on experimentally measured CPU temperature data to predict future CPU temperatures. The predicted temperature is then used to support the adaptive fan control strategy. The heat sink is mounted directly on the CPU of a Raspberry Pi 5 and experimentally evaluated under an extreme CPU workload of approximately 99 percent CPU utilization. The performance of the proposed hybrid system is compared against two benchmark scenarios: passive cooling using PCM embedded in copper foam and a commercial Raspberry Pi 5 active cooler. The proposed heat sink demonstrates superior thermal performance to both benchmarks, achieving peak CPU temperature reductions of approximately 9 C relative to the PCM-copper foam configuration and 6 C relative to the commercial active cooler.
item.dc:creator: Abdallah Ghazal, Fazal Hameed, Elshafey Elshafey, Mohammad Awadallah, Alhasan Emam

item.title: Walk the Cycle: An Efficient Stochastic Solver for Periodic Thermal Analysis of 2.5D/3D ICs
item.description: arXiv:2611.32082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term periodic thermal analysis is essential for designing 2.5D/3D ICs operating under periodic workloads. Deterministic global solvers can be costly for repeated thermal queries, while existing random-walk methods are not tailored to long-term periodic problems or multiscale 3D IC structures, limiting their efficiency and accuracy. We propose CycleWalker, a periodic residual random-walk solver. First, we formulate the periodic steady state (PSS) as an infinite-history backward walk, which needs no initial temperature or warm-up but charges the full temperature field to every path. Second, to cut this cost, we let the walk estimate only the residual of a periodic prior, and shorten long histories by Russian roulette while preserving unbiasedness. Third, since the estimator constrains the prior only to be periodic and piecewise linear in time, we build it at negligible cost by a coarse-grid Fourier solve followed by fine-grid smoothing. Finally, we construct a thermal graph aware of through-silicon vias (TSVs) that bounds the walk's jump rate while retaining the anisotropic conduction of TSV arrays. Experiments on periodic 2.5D/3D IC benchmarks show that, at equal accuracy, CycleWalker achieves up to 75.85X speedup over the transient random-walk solver.
item.dc:creator: Shengnan Cai, Qibo Xue, Tianshu Hou, Tianxiang Zhu, Zixiao Wang, Yibo Lin, Runsheng Wang, Bei Yu

item.title: Beyond Autoregression: Diffusion Language Model is All Analog In-Memory Computing Need
item.description: arXiv:2611.32223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) enables energy-efficient language-model inference, but hardware non-idealities perturb matrix--vector multiplications and degrade generation quality. Autoregressive (AR) models are especially vulnerable: each token is committed to the causal context at birth, so perturbation-induced errors cascade. We study diffusion language models (DLMs), which iteratively refine a masked sequence, as an alternative paradigm. Across scale-matched model pairs and open checkpoints, DLMs degrade more gracefully than AR counterparts under persistent weight perturbations. Controlled analyses rule out cross-round noise averaging and support delayed token commitment and progressive context resolution as the mechanism. A larger denoising-step budget further shrinks the clean--noisy gap, a DLM-specific latency--robustness knob. We perform large-scale simulation tests across diverse datasets and models using a noise model calibrated from real silicon measurements. Furthermore, on a 16-chip 28nm eFlash AIMC cluster, hybrid on-board measurements show DLMs tolerate $1.4$--$3\times$ larger weight noise, making diffusion-based generation a promising paradigm for noise-resilient AIMC inference.
item.dc:creator: Yuanuo Feng, Yubing Ye, Yizhe Chen, Wenshuai Yao, Ngai Wong, Wenyong Zhou, Wang Kang

item.title: Mayfly: Lifecycle-Aware High-Bandwidth Flash for Recursive Self-Improvement
item.description: arXiv:2611.32264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets an LLM improve its agent system by proposing and evaluating candidate variants across tasks. A generation's sessions grow their KV caches together and release them as they finish, creating a burst followed by a decline. At high concurrency, even the KV of sessions ready to run exceeds the GPU's HBM. Offloading that KV to host DRAM or SSDs adds capacity but leaves ready sessions waiting for HBM space before execution. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) can serve the overflow in place, but excessive reads lengthen decode steps and repeated writes consume flash endurance. Our key insight is that where ready KV is read should follow the burst and its decline: from HBF in place while the burst overflows HBM, as much as each step's bandwidth allows, and from HBM again as the decline frees it. A switch between ready and parked decides only whether a block is read, so its flash copy stays valid, and a session's end, which the orchestrator announces, decides when its private KV dies. We present Mayfly, lifecycle-guided HBF management for RSI. Mayfly bounds per-step HBF reads during overflow and returns KV to HBM as sessions finish and free space. It retains a valid backing copy of each block evicted from HBM to avoid rewrites across state transitions, and forwards session-end signals to the controller to avoid copying dead KV during garbage collection. Experimental results show that, at 128 sessions per generation on four added HBF sites, Mayfly finishes 34% sooner than parking the same KV on HBF and 23% sooner than reading it from HBF whenever HBM is full; its gain over parking grows with concurrency, to 55% at 256 sessions on eight sites. Keeping one flash copy per block and trimming at announced session ends avoid write amplification.
item.dc:creator: Chunlin Tian, Mingjia Fan, Feng Yu, Qingyun Zou, Wenju Zhao, Weng-Fai Wong, Bingsheng He

item.title: On the Design of a Slow Control Interlock System for the European GateMate FPGA
item.description: arXiv:2611.32275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Slow Control Systems (SCSs) are essential for the monitoring, configuration, and protection of distributed safety-critical systems in scientific, industrial, and medical applications. Although software-based SCS architectures offer flexibility and scalability, they suffer from software aging and non-deterministic latencies, which limit long-term reliability and timely reaction to critical errors, often requiring additional hardware interlock systems. This paper presents an FPGA-centric lightweight Slow Control Interlock System (SCIS) designed to achieve deterministic ultra-low-latency reaction times in long-running dependable systems. System parameters are acquired and fused at runtime in a Supervisory Monitor Unit (SMU), enabling real-time fault condition classification and prioritization through configurable priority rules and triggering kill-switch actions with microsecond-scale latency. The proposed SMU has been described in VHDL as vendor-agnostic architecture, and assessed on the 28-nm GateMate M1A1 FPGA, using the open-source OSS-CAD-Suite toolchain. Experimental results show that the SMU architecture utilizes only 37,6% of LUTs, 9,4% of FFs, and 35,9% of BRAM. Furthermore, this low resource utilization allow to achieve 40,48 ms reconfiguration time, using OSS-CAD-Suite including gmpack v1.13. This is a key metric for rejuvenation and consequently for enabling aging mitigation in critical applications. Offloading the Ethernet stack to the W5500 Ethernet module and integrating the Grafana dashboard provides a lightweight, deterministic SCIS. This demonstrates the feasibility of our FPGA-centric architecture as a solution to the problem of combining ultra-low-latency interlock capabilities with the scalability of software-based systems.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2026 IEEE Nordic Circuits and Systems Conference (NorCAS)
item.dc:creator: Vitalii Burtsev, Daniele Passaretti, Daniel Anders, Christof Pfannenmueller, Fabian Lurz, Thilo Pionteck

item.title: Trading BRAM for LUTs: Hybrid Bit-Level Weight Storage for FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.32288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an attractive paradigm for energy-efficient AI inference, while their deployment on reconfigurable hardware enables application-specific acceleration without sacrificing model reprogrammability. However, realizing this potential on FPGAs is often severely constrained by the immense on-chip memory needed to store synaptic weights. Existing compression techniques reduce this storage requirement at the cost of weight precision or accuracy. This work presents a hybrid bit-level weight-storage scheme that trades BRAM capacity for FPGA logic resources while preserving the original weights unmodified. Selected weight bits are implemented using Look-Up Tables (LUTs), while the remaining bits are stored in BRAM and jointly reconstructed during inference. We integrate this approach into a spatial dataflow SNN architecture and introduce a practical bit-mapping heuristic that efficiently partitions weight bits between BRAM and LUT-based logic without modifying the weights. Experimental evaluation demonstrates more than 26% reduction in BRAM utilization with a modest increase in LUT and register usage, resulting in significant overall power savings.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Sekertzis, Giorgos Dimitrakopoulos

item.title: Scaling Architectural Simulation to Giga Instructions Per Second
item.description: arXiv:2611.32397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The cost of detailed architectural simulation constrains design-space exploration, while parallelization across simulated cores offers limited host concurrency for single-core and small multicore targets. We present GIPSim, an instruction-driven simulator that derives instruction timing from dependencies and resource constraints, reducing the overhead of updating pipeline state every simulated cycle. It applies synchronization-guided temporal decomposition to recorded execution, exposing host parallelism beyond the target core count. GIPSim replays the resulting segments in parallel and aggregates their durations through a dependency graph to estimate overall execution time, with replay contexts reconstructed using retained microarchitectural state, warmup, and synchronization-guided cache eviction. This accounts for synchronization waits without requiring host workers to follow target execution order. We evaluate GIPSim using QEMU traces of application and operating system execution on multi-core x86-64, AArch64, and RV64GC systems. GIPSim achieves an average single-node simulation throughput of 13.8 million instructions per second (MIPS) with one worker and 1{,}010 MIPS with 96 workers, peaking at 1{,}421 MIPS. The corresponding mean absolute percentage errors in execution cycles relative to gem5 are 7.52\% and 7.43\%, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Zhouyi Shen, Hao Tang, Ruike Liu, Jingwei Sun, Guangzhong Sun

item.title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.
item.dc:creator: Yuisei Iwata, Yutaka Masuda, Tohru Ishihara

item.title: OpenWoud: Vendor-Unlocked Scalable Adaptive Random Forest Accelerator
item.description: arXiv:2611.32662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online Machine Learning (ML) enables real-time decision-making on evolving data streams. These dynamic models learn continuously to adapt to new concepts, as previous ones become invalid, but their performance is often limited by throughput. The Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) is a state-of-the-art model for this setting, which naturally exposes parallelism and is therefore well-suited for hardware acceleration. However, prior Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based accelerators are vendor-locked and rely on resource-hungry Floating-Point (FP) arithmetics, limiting their scalability and portability. We present OpenWoud, a vendor-unlocked ARF framework for FPGAs. Our design replaces FP operators with a flexible FiXed-Point (FxP) arithmetic library and introduces fully transparent, manually scheduled dataflows for training and drift detection. This enables fine-grained time/area trade-offs and predictable behavior across platforms. A comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets shows that OpenWoud maintains or increases accuracy (up to +12.89%), compared to a prior FPGA accelerator, while reducing the resource utilization by half. Competitive performance is observed compared to GPU (0.5 - 1.5x speed-up) and an FPGA baseline (0.2 - 0.5x), despite the latter being based on idealized simulation. Crucially, OpenWoud sustains true sample-by-sample inference, unlike GPUs that require batch insertion.
item.dc:creator: Ewout van Nimwegen, Elijah Seth Cishugi, Hendrik Folmer, Marco Ottavi, Kuan-Hsun Chen

item.title: Discovering Bandwidth-Efficient Prefetchers to Shrink the Cache Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2611.31983v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Shared last-level caches (LLCs) increasingly dominate server processor die area, forcing architects to trade core counts for cache capacity. While intelligent data prefetching offers a pathway to reclaim this silicon, designing coordinated, multi-level prefetching policies for multi-core systems is bottlenecked by day-long, cycle-level simulations. This simulation wall limits even LLM-based microarchitecture discovery; the state-of-the-art ArchAgent system evolves one cache level at a time on single-core benchmarks, adds multi-core configurations only at the end, and trails the human champion under multi-core shared cache contention. We introduce DuoArchitect, an autonomous agentic framework for multi-fidelity, multi-core co-discovery of prefetchers. Agents jointly evolve evaluation proxies and coordinated prefetching policies across the L1D, L2, and LLC hierarchies, constructing simulation proxies 3-26x faster than cluster evaluation and hardware diagnostic oracles to guide the search. To study how much cache silicon a smarter prefetcher can replace, we evaluate and evolve prefetchers under reduced cache budgets, and find that evolving under our tightest cache constraint (with both the L2 and LLC halved) produced our strongest prefetcher overall at every cache size we tested: DuoArch-Nano. On the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4) benchmarks with full-size caches, DuoArch-Nano delivers a 9.2% geomean IPC speedup (+10.5% on four-core mixes) while reducing four-core DRAM traffic by 11.4%, more than doubling the gains of the human champion BertiGO and the agentic ArchAgent v2. When the LLC is halved, DuoArch-Nano erases the baseline's 8.6% overall slowdown and edges out the full-LLC baseline overall (+0.88%), showing that agentic frameworks can generate prefetchers that reclaim megabytes of LLC SRAM per core with zero overall IPC penalty.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Tser Jern Kon, Akanksha Jain, Abraham Gonzalez, Rui Meng, Dilara Soylu, Shubham Agarwal, Yawen Wang, Iman Hosseini, Hanna Alam, Jinsung Yoon, Tomas Pfister, Nanyun Peng, Chun-Liang Li, Parthasarathy Ranganathan

item.title: APQKE-DR: Entropy-Failure Analysis of a Post-Quantum-Initialized Ratcheted Channel
item.description: arXiv:2611.32024v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-lived secure channels for embedded and cyber-physical systems (CPSs) must resist quantum attacks and failures in endpoint randomness. While several post-quantum key exchange protocols exist, their security assumes reliable randomness at the endpoint, but this assumption is not always true in embedded devices. In this paper, we introduce the Entropy Attack Suite (EAS) to evaluate secure channels facing endpoint randomness failures, such as low-entropy boot and Random Number Generation (RNG) path subversion. As a case study, we design and implement APQKE-DR, a post-quantum secure channel. Its handshake uses ML-KEM [1] and ML-DSA [2], producing a root key for an X25519 Double Ratchet. We assess the performance of APQKE-DR and security for smart grid communication, and integrate it beneath ANSI C12.22 and DNP3 without altering payload formats. On a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, the APQKE handshake exchanges 9,610 bytes with median latencies of 1.99 ms (node) and 0.82 ms (server). The ratcheted channel adds 31 bytes per message. With fresh randomness and ideal cryptographic primitives, ProVerif verifies the modeled secrecy and authentication properties. If randomness fails, EAS can recover the RNG stream and root key from public transcripts. Under RNG-path subversion, a weak generator exposes the root key across sessions. If subversion also affects X25519 keys, attackers may access ratchet keys and plaintexts. TPM seeding prevents early-boot attacks but not later subversion, while measured boot can block modified firmware. Secure deployment thus requires integrity along the entire entropy path, not just strong cryptographic primitives.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Asfand Hafeez, Zain Ul Abideen, Amna Zafar, Kazi Hassan Shakib, Arslan Munir

item.title: Power Side-Channel Evaluation using Multi-FPGA Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.32652v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Complex out-of-order processors are difficult to evaluate for power side-channel leakage before tapeout. A single FPGA often lacks sufficient capacity, whereas conventional CAD-based analysis is too slow to support the large numbers of traces required by practical attacks. Multi-FPGA emulation provides greater capacity, but existing partitioning schemes are not security-aware and thus results in poor attack performance. This work presents Scissors, a security-aware multi-FPGA partitioning approach for pre-silicon power side-channel evaluation of complex out-of-order processors. Scissors uses side-channel vulnerability factor (SVF) analysis to identify signals correlated with the secret key. It then keeps strongly key-correlated signals confined to one FPGA partition (measured) while moving rest of the signals to the other FPGAs (support), improving the observability of the side-channel information. We evaluate Scissors through RTL simulations and physical measurements on a two-U200 FPGA testbed, using frequency-domain CPA with a Hamming-weight leakage model. RTL ablation shows that only 68-71 high-SVF signals dominate key recovery process. For a single-core processor (SingleBOOM), Scissors recovers the key with 12,000 traces, compared with 49,000 for the unpartitioned design and 43,000 for TritonPart, while improving correct-key correlation by $2.83\times$. For a quad-core processor (QuadBOOM), which exceeds the capacity of the CW340 single-FPGA platform, Scissors reduces the required traces from 111,000 to 66,000 and improves correlation by $1.48\times$ over TritonPart. Scissors also reduces QuadBOOM RTL-to-bitstream generation from 61 h 39 min to 6 h 40 min, a $9.25\times$ speedup. These results show that security-aware partitioning improves leakage observability and attack performance while substantially reducing implementation time for complex processors against the baseline method.
item.dc:creator: Yaswanth Tavva, Geng Luo, Trevor E. Carlson, Li-Shiuan Peh

item.title: Enabling Mixed criticality applications for the Versal AI-Engines
item.description: arXiv:2604.21124v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixed-criticality systems (MCSs) are used in autonomous driving, aviation and medical systems. They require hardware platforms, which are reconfigurable at runtime to fully utilize performance while maintaining critical deadlines in emergency scenarios. However, Systems-on-Chip (SoC) components, like the Versal AI-Engine (AIE), only support static task mapping, limiting its utilization. In this work, we propose a dynamic task dispatching infrastructure that enables task switching on the AIE at runtime. Based on this infrastructure, we present an MCS design that dynamically assigns tasks of different criticality to AIE tiles, depending on the criticality mode of the system. Our approach overcomes the limitations of static dataflow graph mappings and, for the first time, exploits the parallel processing capabilities of the AIE for MCSs. We provide a timing analysis of the overhead introduced by the task dispatching infrastructure, which demonstrates that it is negligible. This makes it suitable for MCSs, as upper bounds can be identified. Finally, we evaluate the proposed infrastructure using an autonomous driving workload with tasks that have variable execution times and different criticality levels. In this case study, we maximized AIE utilization, reducing idle time by 65.5\%, while measuring an execution time overhead of less than 0.8\%, and doubling the throughput of low-criticality tasks.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2026 IEEE Nordic Circuits and Systems Conference (NorCAS)
item.dc:creator: Vincent Sprave, Martin Wilhelm, Daniele Passaretti, Alberto Garcia-Ortiz, Thilo Pionteck

item.title: Decoupling Logical Masks from GPU Execution for Dynamic Block-Sparse Attention
item.description: arXiv:2609.25869v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Attention computation makes inference expensive in video diffusion transformers (vDiTs), which generate videos through iterative denoising. Block-sparse attention (BSA) reduces this cost by computing only blocks selected by a logical mask, which specifies the attention interactions to compute. Existing BSA runtimes either fix one physical execution plan per block geometry, which limits adaptation to varying masks and graphics processing units (GPUs), or plan each mask at runtime, which adds preparation overhead to every request. Because masks change across requests, this per-mask planning must be repeated, so its cost can outweigh the execution-time savings. We present Tessera, a runtime for dynamic BSA that decouples logical masks from GPU execution through two-layer physical execution plans that preserve the specified attention interactions. First, its physical mapping layer retains, combines, or subdivides logical blocks into physical tiles suited to different mask shapes and GPU architectures. Second, its task organization layer groups and schedules tiles within GPU tasks to reuse data, expose parallelism, and overlap data movement with computation. Third, its plan selector chooses a plan for each request with low overhead, through either a plan table built from offline profiling or a calibrated cost model, which extends selection to masks outside the profiled distribution and to a new GPU with about 100 calibration requests. Implemented with specialized CUDA kernels for four NVIDIA GPU generations and evaluated on 2,312 real attention masks and two video diffusion models, Tessera achieves up to $2.88\times$ BSA request speedup over baseline systems in these models and speeds up their 50-step loop by $1.21$--$1.24\times$.
item.dc:creator: Shanghao Liu, Xiaoyun Yu, Wanting Li, Wenqi Jiang

item.title: Lachesis: Lifetime-Aware KV Cache Placement for Agent Serving across HBM and High-Bandwidth Flash
item.description: arXiv:2610.08378v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In agent serving, agents and their sub-agents accumulate context as KV cache across many requests, far beyond HBM capacity. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) adds greater capacity at HBM-class read bandwidth, allowing a server to grow its batch and throughput under a relaxed SLO. We show that this gain meets an endurance wall as the batch growth wears HBF out within its warranty period. Prior work analyzes which KV should reach HBF assuming a request's KV remains readable until completion. However, an agent run is stateful, and by design, its harness discards parts of the context throughout the run. We find that the context divides into groups of KV that the harness discards together, so each group shares one lifetime that is known before the group is written. These lifetimes differ on three axes: reasoning stripped when the next user message ends a turn, a sub-agent's context discarded when it returns, and how long each sub-agent runs, which can be ranked when it starts. Guided by this characterization, we present Lachesis, a lifetime-aware KV cache placement layer that chooses HBM or HBF for each group when the group is written. In simulation of an eight-GPU B200 server on multi-agent traces, HBF with Lachesis serves 7.61-9.16$\times$ the throughput of the better of an HBM-only server and a DGX server with host DDR5. On the same traces, Lachesis extends HBF lifetime by 1.14-4.17$\times$ over HBM-first placement, which fills HBM before HBF. Since Lachesis keeps short-lived KV in HBM, a server running it can use more HBM stacks per GPU within the warranty. Our design-space exploration finds that Lachesis at 3/5 HBM/HBF stacks per GPU serves the highest throughput among the configurations that attach HBF directly to the GPU and outlast the warranty.
item.dc:creator: Jaehoon Yang, Jeongmin Lee, Haneul Park, Seung Yul Lee, Nam Sung Kim, Jae W. Lee

item.title: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
item.description: arXiv:2611.23022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. Under NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), the bank access and the tag lookup each open a covert channel across processes, whose rate rises with each GPU generation. Also under MPS, this starvation lets one warp slow a colocated cuBLAS matrix multiplication by up to 750x on the A100 and 563x on the H100.
item.dc:creator: Wenbo Han, Pierre Talbot

item.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
item.description: arXiv:2611.24637v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.
item.dc:creator: Guilherme Guedes, Marco P. Apolinario, Charlotte Frenkel

item.title: Learning in the Passive Space: End-to-End Muti-Order Port-Hamiltonian Macromodeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.28778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Compact, passive state-space macromodels of interconnects and power-delivery networks are essential for stable transient signal- and power-integrity simulations. However, conventional flows require costly per-layout full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, while both traditional fitting and prior learning surrogates rely on post-hoc fitting or passivity perturbation that degrades accuracy without guaranteeing convergence. In this work, we propose an end-to-end macromodeling framework that learns directly in the passive space, mapping physical layout graphs to multi-order port-Hamiltonian (pH) macromodels. Specifically, our network encodes each layout graph into unconstrained matrix blocks and assembles them via a complete, prefix-nested pH parameterization that guarantees continuous-frequency passivity and stability by construction, yielding valid $k$-state macromodels via direct state slicing in one forward pass. To train all orders without reference realizations, we supervise the network directly on S-parameters through a progressive order-growth curriculum. Evaluated on 27k unseen test structures from a 270k-structure advanced-packaging dataset, our framework reduces mean S-parameter error by $42\%$ on average (up to $65\%$) over established macromodeling tools fitted to ground-truth EM responses, achieves zero passivity violations across $459{,}000$ exported models, and accelerates macromodel generation by $11{,}000$--$39{,}000\times$ ($36$--$85$~ms per layout).
item.dc:creator: Benchao Zhu, Keren Zhu
